intro: The story of Babel is short, only nine verses in Genesis 11. People build a tower. Their language gets mixed up, and they are scattered. Right before it, Genesis 10 lists about seventy nations. Right after it, God calls one man, Abram. This unit reads these chapters together, beside other old texts.

You will read old copies of Deuteronomy 32:8 from the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek Septuagint. You will meet old Jewish books, like Jubilees, Sirach and the history of Josephus. You will also meet modern scholars, like Mark S. Smith and Michael Heiser. They do not all agree, and you will see why.

By the end, you will be able to retell the Babel story and compare old copies of Deuteronomy 32:8. You will describe how different readers explain the gods of the nations. You will also trace the promise to Abram, that all families of the earth would be blessed, and explain how Jewish and Christian readers understand it.
bigQuestion: What happened to the nations after Babel, and how did the promise to Abram speak to them, as ancient and modern readers see it?

timeline.t: The great ziggurat of Ur is built in southern Mesopotamia
Scribes at Ugarit write clay tablets about the god El and his seventy sons
Jewish scholars in Egypt begin the Septuagint, a Greek translation of the Torah
The book of Jubilees retells Babel and Abram turning from idols
A copy of Deuteronomy reading sons of God is made, later found among the Dead Sea Scrolls
Paul writes Galatians, linking the promise to Abraham with the nations
Josephus finishes his Antiquities of the Jews, retelling Babel and Abraham
Genesis Rabbah gathers Jewish teachings on Genesis, including Abram and the idols
The Leningrad Codex, the oldest complete Masoretic Hebrew Bible, is copied
Rashi in France explains Deuteronomy 32:8 as the seventy of Jacob's family
Mark S. Smith publishes The Origins of Biblical Monotheism, comparing Ugarit and the Bible
Michael Heiser publishes The Unseen Realm, with his reading of Babel and Deuteronomy 32

words.d: the city in Genesis 11 where languages were mixed up; its name sounds like the Hebrew word for mix up
a tall tower built in steps beside a temple in ancient Mesopotamia
the list of peoples in Genesis 10, about seventy in the Hebrew text
an old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Egypt around 250 BCE
the standard Hebrew text of the Bible, carefully copied by Jewish scribes called the Masoretes
very old scrolls found in caves near the Dead Sea starting in 1947
a Hebrew word that can mean God, gods, or other spirit beings
God's heavenly court: the spirit beings around God's throne, as in Psalm 82
a share that belongs to someone; Deuteronomy 32:9 calls Israel the LORD's portion
a binding agreement; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel
a gift of good things, or words that wish someone good
an old Jewish book, written around 150 BCE, that retells the stories of Genesis and early Exodus

test.q: Where does the Babel story take place?
test.why: Genesis 11:2 places the story on a plain in Shinar, an old name for southern Mesopotamia.

test.q: What does the name Babel sound like in Hebrew?
test.why: Babel sounds like balal, the Hebrew word for mix up.

test.q: About how many nations are in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10?
test.why: Readers count about seventy nations in the Hebrew text of the Table of Nations.

choices: A tall stepped tower beside a temple
test.why: A ziggurat was a stepped temple-tower in Mesopotamia. Many scholars think Babel's tower was pictured this way.

test.q: What does the Masoretic Text say in Deuteronomy 32:8?
test.why: The Masoretic Text says sons of Israel. A Dead Sea Scroll says sons of God.

test.q: Which old copy of Deuteronomy 32:8 says sons of God?
choices: A Dead Sea Scroll found near the Dead Sea
test.why: A Dead Sea Scroll copy says sons of God. The Leningrad Codex and the King James say sons of Israel.

test.q: In Heiser's reading, who ruled the nations after Babel?
choices: Lesser elohim, the sons of God
test.why: Heiser read Deuteronomy 32:8–9 to say God set the nations under lesser elohim and kept Israel as his own.

test.q: Which ancient historian said Nimrod led the builders of the tower?
test.why: Josephus, in his Antiquities of the Jews (c. 94 CE), named Nimrod as the leader. Genesis 11 names no leader.

test.q: What three things did God tell Abram to leave?
choices: His tent, his camels and his sheep
His country, his relatives and his father's house
His city, his temple and his king
His tower, his bricks and his tar
test.why: Genesis 12:1 names his country, his relatives and his father's house.

test.q: Which verse says Abram's ancestors served other gods?
test.why: Joshua 24:2 says Terah and Abram's other ancestors served other gods.

test.q: Which Hebrew word appears in both Genesis 11:4 and Genesis 12:2?
test.why: The builders want to make a shem, a name, and God promises to make Abram's shem great.

test.q: Which verse asks God to rise up because he will inherit all the nations?
test.why: Psalm 82:8 asks God to rise up and judge the earth, because he will inherit all the nations.

choices: As sons of God who ruled the nations
As sons of Israel, the seventy of Jacob's family
As the seventy sons of El
test.why: Rashi followed sons of Israel and linked it to the seventy of Jacob's family who went to Egypt.

test.q: Which New Testament verse says the good news was told to Abraham ahead of time?
test.why: In Galatians 3:8, Paul says the Scripture told the good news to Abraham ahead of time.

test.q: Which old book says God set a ruler over every nation, but Israel is the Lord's portion?
test.why: Sirach 17:17 says God set a ruler over every people, but Israel is the Lord's portion, like Deuteronomy 32:9.

write.prompt: Did God give up on the nations after Babel? Use at least two passages from this unit, such as Genesis 11:1–9, Deuteronomy 32:8–9, Sirach 17:17, Genesis 12:1–3 or Psalm 82:8. Tell what each passage says. Then explain how two readers understood it, such as Rashi, Jubilees, Mark Smith or Michael Heiser.
tips: Name the book, chapter and verse each time you use a passage.
Say who holds each idea: Rashi read, Heiser argued, many Christians believe.
Compare the readings. You do not need to pick a winner.
Use terms from this unit, like elohim, portion and Table of Nations.
